p.s: Every year, small businesses lose contracts they were fully qualified to win.
Not on price. Not on quality of work. On a technicality — a missing certificate, an insurance minimum that's a few thousand dollars short, a signature page nobody noticed was required.

Reading a dense RFP, checking it line by line against your own paperwork, and writing a tailored proposal can take hours — hours a business owner should be spending running the business, or bidding on the next contract.

This is BidWright — an agent built with the Strands Agents SDK that reads the RFP, checks your company against every requirement, drafts the proposal, and only asks you to decide the things only you can decide.
BidWright is built for the people who respond to RFPs regularly, but don't have a dedicated compliance team to do it:
municipal contractors, landscapers, janitorial and facilities companies, IT and managed-service providers, construction subcontractors — office managers and owners who are the entire back office.
What used to take an afternoon of cross-referencing now runs unattended.

And because the compliance check never claims something is met unless your own paperwork actually backs it up, you're not just saving time — you're not losing a winnable bid to a mistake you didn't catch.
Let's watch it work on a real example: a municipal landscaping RFP, and a small landscaping company's actual capability profile.

One click, and an orchestrator agent takes over — coordinating specialized sub-agents, each returning validated, structured data instead of loose text one agent might hand the next and get wrong. The activity log below is streaming real tool calls as they happen, not a canned animation.

The Compliance Checker compares every requirement against the company's actual profile — insurance certificates, licenses, staff qualifications — and on this run it correctly caught the company's general liability insurance sitting at one million dollars when the RFP requires two million per occurrence, plus a missing signed cover letter and a missing pricing schedule. Real gaps, precisely identified.

Right after that, a second, completely independent auditor agent re-derives its own compliance verdict from scratch — it never sees the first check's answer. Any disagreement between the two is never quietly resolved in favor of either one; it gets forced into needs review so a human decides, not a coin flip between two model calls.

Before a proposal ever reaches a human, it passes a critic agent that checks the drafted text against the compliance report itself — catching, on a real run, the drafted letter claiming "we carry all required insurance" while the report showed that exact coverage as a blocking gap — plus a guardrail scan for overclaiming language. Nothing is auto-submitted: the run lands here, in an approval panel, and a human has to actually click Approve.
And you can ask it questions directly — this chat is grounded only in that job's own generated files, so if the answer isn't in there, it says so instead of guessing.
Everything funnels into exactly one place a busy owner actually needs to read: Decisions Needed.
One summary. Either "ready to submit," or here are the specific blocking gaps and what closes each one.
BidWright drafts. It doesn't submit — a human always reviews and signs off, which is the entire point of that approval panel.

And this is just the core loop — the same run also checks for a teaming partner when a gap can't be closed alone, flags when an RFP amendment invalidates a proposal already in progress, and tracks recurring gaps across a company's bid history.
BidWright — built with the Strands Agents SDK, for the Agents for Humans Hackathon. Read the RFP once. Draft with confidence.
